# A graph that grows itself: what a knowledge graph is worth when nobody is there to query it

> Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.

## Abstract

Ultrastable R&D (Ultrastable): The common view is that a knowledge graph is a search aid: you build it, then someone queries it. Microsoft's GraphRAG work (Edge and others, 2024) showed graphs help most on questions about a whole corpus, by grouping entities into communities and summarising each one. LightRAG and HippoRAG pushed the same idea toward cheaper, incremental updates. Link prediction and Swanson's old literature-based discovery go further: the useful output is the missing edge. Ashby's ultrastable system needs exactly that kind of signal, a measure that tells the second loop when the first one is stuck. So we built the graph into every system Ultrastable runs. Each tick reads only rows past a cursor, pulls out ids, rule tags and file paths without a model, then has a small model name the entities and relations in those new rows, embeds them, and summarizes each community whose members changed. The spend throttle slows this down; it never switches it off. A pair that reads alike, has no edge and shares no neighbour becomes a lead. Two leads a day at most become work items. A lead counts as kept only when a later change links the pair for real. Most graph work assumes a person asks a question and the graph helps answer it. We test the other use: a system that builds the graph from everything it writes down, looks for pairs that read alike but are not linked, files each one as work, and counts how many turn out to be real. 1 of 1 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## The study

Can a system find connections in its own records that nobody asked it to find?. Ultrastable R&D, Ultrastable; own R&D question set, read against the published work on graph retrieval and link prediction and regenerated from this system's own graph, version 2026-11-25. Data: The core knowledge graph this system rebuilds every day from its own work items, studies and rules (ops/kgraph), and the leads it files and settles (ops/kgraph/leads.jsonl).

## Findings, mechanisms and measurements

### K1. The graph keeps itself current (systems)

**The study:** Every system Ultrastable runs keeps a knowledge graph of its own data, built and refreshed by its own tick, with no setup. (Graph build)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- KGRAPH-1 (`foundation/datagraph.py`): the daily build reads every work item, study and rule, and a probe fails when the graph is over 36 hours old
- KGRAPH-1 (`seed/worker/src/graphai.js`): each tick Worker reads only rows past its cursor and files KG-LAG when it falls behind

**Measured here:** share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending: 1.0 (n = 5). Target >= 1. Verdict: **met**.
Source: doctrine/knowledge-graph.json (declared).

## Limits

- Extraction. Every tick Worker now asks a small Workers AI model to name the entities and relations in its new rows, a few records per call, and embeds them in one batched call. The repository half that builds the core graph in CI still extracts ids, tags, paths and terms only.
- Communities. Communities come from label propagation, not the Leiden clustering GraphRAG uses, and only communities whose membership changed are summarized again. The model's summaries are proposals and are not checked against the records yet.
- Cost. AI work is scaled by the account's spend level and capped at a share of the included daily allocation; the neuron counts are estimates per call, recorded per system per day, not a meter reading.
- Yield is young. A lead needs days to be acted on, so the kept share starts near zero and only means something after a few weeks of filings.
